items.title: Glucoregulatory and Inflammatory Trajectories in Pregnancy with Obesity: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Exercise Trial
items.summary: Objective: To evaluate moderate-intensity exercise effects on glucoregulatory and inflammatory markers in pregnant women with obesity. Methods: Secondary analysis of the Expecting Study (NCT02125149) included 263 sedentary pregnant women with pre-pregnancy BMI [>=]30kg/m2 randomized to exercise (EX, n=157) or standard-of-care (SoC, n=106). Fasting biomarkers were assessed at 12.14{+/-}0.50, 24.19{+/-}0.68, and 36.03{+/-}0.58 weeks ' gestation. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated intervention and gestational effects at 24-36 weeks. Exploratory repeated-measures continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) included 18 participants (SoC=6, EX=12), evaluating 24-h/temporal glycemia and exploring inflammatory marker associations. Results: Insulin, C-peptide, HOMA2-IR, HOMA2-%B, IL-6, and TNF- increased with gestation, while HOMA2-%S and CRP decreased (all p 95% valid wear time; glycemia remained normoglycemic. By 36-weeks, SoC-metrics declined in 24-h and nocturnal glucose and time-in-range (TIR), with increased time-below-range (all p<0.022). TIR was inversely associated with IL-6 at 24-weeks (-0.23 [95%CI: -0.43,-0.02] p=0.035), and mean amplitude of glycemic excursion positively with TNF- at 36-weeks (0.02 [95%CI: 0.00,0.04] p=0.033). Conclusion: Exercise did not modify mid-to late-gestation fasting glucoregulatory or inflammatory profiles. High CGM-adherence and preliminary indications of distinct longitudinal glycemic patterns support further CGM evaluation in antepartum behavioral interventions.

items.title: Digital Twin Workflow for Continuous Glucose Forecasting: Real-Time Data Assimilation Using Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Digital twins for physiological forecasting require robust mechanisms for continuously assimilating streaming data and adapting to patient-specific dynamics. Threshold-triggered model updates can restore predictive performance after substantial drift, but their reactive nature limits continuous adaptation. We propose a proactive digital twin framework that couples a pretrained PatchTST foundation model with an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning (RL) agent for residual correction. Using a 30-minute look-back window and recent residual history, the agent generates bounded corrections ({+/-} 0.05) to the first-step baseline forecast, with corrected predictions recursively propagated over a 15-step horizon. We evaluate both an RL-only workflow and a hybrid workflow combining RL correction with threshold-triggered fine-tuning using minute-by-minute continuous glucose monitoring data from 10 critically ill patients with sepsis. Across all patients, the pretrained RL agent improves forecasting accuracy without patient-specific retraining. Both workflows reduce trajectory-averaged mean absolute percentage error, ensemble relative error, and maximum errors compared with the uncorrected baseline and previously developed reactive digital twin models. These findings support residual reinforcement learning as a lightweight mechanism for continuous, real-time data assimilation that preserves the foundation model's global predictive prior while enabling patient-specific forecast adaptation, with potential applications in critical care decision support.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6742: A Feasibility Study for Integrating Schumann Resonance Monitoring, Geomagnetic Activity Indices, and Large-Scale Ambulatory ECG Databases: Toward Synchronized Environmental-Physiological Research
items.summary: Schumann resonance (SR) is a global electromagnetic phenomenon generated within the Earth-ionosphere cavity, with a fundamental frequency near 7.83 Hz. Whether SR dynamics are associated with human autonomic nervous system activity as indexed by heart rate variability (HRV) remains an open empirical question. Addressing this question rigorously requires (a) large-scale, time-synchronized physiological datasets, (b) continuous SR monitoring with precise timestamps, and (c) control for geomagnetic activity (Kp index) as a major confounding variable. Currently available open datasets do not yet satisfy condition (a). Rather than forcing premature physiological conclusions, this paper presents a feasibility and methodology study that characterizes each data source, demonstrates the analysis pipeline on representative data, and identifies the design requirements for a future definitive study. Frequency-domain HRV indices were characterized using approximately 730,000 24-h Holter ECG recordings from the Allostatic State Mapping by Ambulatory ECG Repository (ALLSTAR). Broadband voltage SD (segment-wise standard deviation of AC-coupled voltage, used solely as a descriptive amplitude proxy) was characterized using the publicly available Mendeley Schumann Resonance Dataset (35 min segments, 525,000 samples each). A partial correlation framework that controls for the NOAA Kp geomagnetic index is proposed and evaluated through simulation on representative parameter sets. Because the HRV and SR datasets were not collected at the same time or location, no direct physiological inference is drawn from their comparison. The reported association statistics are illustrative demonstrations of the pipeline applied to representative data, not empirical evidence of SR-HRV coupling. These findings define the data requirements and analytical methodology for future synchronized SR-HRV-Kp studies.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6710: An ESP32-S3 Multimodal Wearable Sensor Platform with Embedded XGBoost for Focal-to-Bilateral Tonic-Clonic Seizure Detection and IoT Alerting
items.summary: Wearable seizure-detection systems can provide objective event monitoring and rapid caregiver alerting without continuous bedside observation. This study presents a resource-constrained multimodal wearable sensor platform for focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (FBTCS) detection using edge artificial intelligence and Internet of Things (IoT) communication. The prototype integrates an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, an analog electromyography (EMG) channel, an MPU6050 inertial sensor, MAX30102 photoplethysmography, GPS, a TFT display, local vibration/buzzer outputs, and Blynk cloud telemetry. The seizure-decision path uses synchronized EMG and acceleration acquired at 100 Hz in non-overlapping 10 s windows. EMG and acceleration are resampled for compatibility with the reference feature pipeline, 13 statistical features are extracted from each modality (26 total), and an 85-tree XGBoost model is executed locally. A probability threshold of 0.85 is combined with temporal smoothing, consecutive-window confirmation, and a 60 s refractory interval. Software verification showed maximum absolute probability differences of approximately 1.19 x 10-7 for random feature-vector tests and 1.49 x 10-8 for end-to-end recorded windows relative to the Python reference. Within the reported validation record covering 2643.69 h and 18 record-labeled FBTCS events, 12 events were detected (12/18; 67% sensitivity). Precision was approximately 26%, F1-score approximately 38%, the reported false-alarm rate was 0.31 per 24 h, and median detection latency was 61.5 s. Approximately 34 false alarms are estimated from the reported false-alarm rate and evaluation duration; this is an estimated count rather than a percentage or directly observed count. Hardware, local alarm, display, GPS, and cloud communication functions passed functional integration tests. The small event count, uncertain label provenance, low precision, and long latency mean that these data support an engineering proof-of-concept

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6670: The Case for Low-Friction High-Adherence Passive Sleep-Tracking Devices in Longitudinal Monitoring of Neurodegenerative Disease
items.summary: Digital health technologies are playing an increasingly important role in patient monitoring, able to capture longitudinal data to supplement scheduled episodic evaluations conducted by clinicians. Rapid advances in sensors and data processing algorithms have resulted in some highly sophisticated systems capable of monitoring and tracking numerous symptoms with high levels of sensitivity and specificity. These approaches, however, often require active engagement with the patient, potentially increasing burden in a clinical trial and often resulting in diminishing adherence over time. In the case of slow-progressing neurodegenerative diseases, this may become an obstacle, as often very subtle changes in symptoms are typically monitored over a multi-year period. Accordingly, there is evident interest in passive monitoring solutions which have minimal burden on patients. Smart ring technologies are one such solution, with appealing form factors, low engagement requirements and increasing intervals before device recharging is required. While newer devices are capable of tracking sleep function with increasing levels of accuracy, they are unable to offer the precision afforded by gold standard sleep analysis such as electroencephalography (EEG), polysomnography (PSG) and sleep laboratory protocols. Prompted by a recent study which highlighted the reduced accuracy of consumer-based sleep devices compared with conventional approaches, we posit that the benefits of such devices may offset the constraints of measurement accuracy. Furthermore, any accuracy-adherence trade-offs would be compensated by long-term statistical benefits derived from detecting within-person changes and reducing measurement noise through enhanced sampling frequencies. In this perspective, we highlight their potential utility in tracking Parkinson's disease patients longitudinally, where compromised sleep architectures are associated with multiple symptoms and continuous monitoring could offer myriad

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6683: A Human-in-the-Loop Reference-Label Curation Framework for Task Classification During Free-Living, Using 3D Animation of IMU Data
items.summary: Reference-labelled data for training activity-recognition models from wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) are typically collected in laboratories, which poorly represent real-world movement, and often use video, which raises privacy concerns and does not scale to long recordings. This study evaluated a novel human-in-the-loop annotation framework in which IMU-derived skeletal animations are reviewed by human raters to generate activity labels. Eight participants performed 72 functional tasks in a simulated living environment while wearing IMUs, with synchronized video serving as a reference standard. Data from five participants were analyzed. Two reviewers labelled both IMU animations and video recordings, and intra- and inter-reviewer agreement were compared across a detailed label set and a simplified four-class taxonomy. Using the video annotations as the reference standard, the intra-reviewer macro-averaged F1 for the detailed label set was 61.9 +/- 13.5% (Cohen's = 0.67 +/- 0.12), and 78.0 +/- 11.5% ( = 0.74 +/- 0.13) for the simplified taxonomy. In a sensitivity analysis excluding samples labelled as transitions, macro-F1 was 69.4 +/- 10.9% and 92.8 +/- 5.3%, respectively. Inter-reviewer agreement for the detailed label set was lower when labelling animations ( = 0.51 +/- 0.06) than video ( = 0.72 +/- 0.02). A main source of disagreement between reviewers was in the labelling of transitions of state, reflecting in part the ambiguous nature of defining their endpoints. These findings support skeletal-animation review as a potential privacy-preserving alternative to video annotation for generating reference labels in simulated living; validation in free-living recordings, and of the reconstructed kinematics, is still required.

items.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
items.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6665: A Multimodal IMU-RTLS Manufacturing Motion Dataset for Worker Activity Recognition
items.summary: Worker Activity Recognition can improve operational visibility in human-centric manufacturing systems. However, existing approaches remain limited by scarce industrial datasets, isolated task recordings, and sensor-intensive configurations. This study presents two multimodal datasets and a cyber-physical architecture for complementary levels of worker motion. The Gross Worker Activity Recognition dataset targets operator proximity to workstation and the identification of logistic activities in reconfigurable manufacturing systems. It contains 814,065 positioning samples from eight production setups, each repeated twice, involving more than 40 workers. This dataset is benchmarked with different learning structure algorithms, and the Long Short-Term Memory is selected as a baseline model, achieving an F1-score of 86%. The Fine Worker Activity Recognition dataset targets the segmentation of five pump-assembly operations using two inertial measurement units and a radio-frequency-identification smart glove. It comprises approximately 7 h of recordings and more than one million samples from 50 complete assemblies performed by three workers. Transformer, ResNet, and SqueezeNet models are benchmarked, with SqueezeNet selected as the baseline after achieving the highest F1-score of 85.2%. Moreover, the results identify transition-rich activities as the principal recognition bottleneck and show how complementary motion levels support different manufacturing indicators.

items.title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
items.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

items.title: ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health
items.summary: Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.

items.title: Contactless gait-derived features as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents
items.summary: Timely assessment of depression severity in adolescents is essential for guiding clinical care, yet conventional evaluations rely on episodic clinical assessments and symptom rating scales. Contactless gait analysis offers a potentially scalable approach to capturing objective behavioral features associated with depression. Here, we introduce the Long-Distance 3D Adolescent Depression Gait Dataset (LD3D-ADG), comprising depth-sensor gait recordings from 119 adolescents at a single center, including 39 healthy controls, 41 with mild depression, and 39 with moderate-to-severe depression. We developed UMLPA-GCN, a graph convolutional network that models spatiotemporal gait dynamics across three anatomically defined skeletal partitions. In participant-independent five-fold cross-validation, UMLPA-GCN achieved 75.63% classification accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 75.52%, and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.839 (95% confidence interval, 0.779--0.899). Class-specific recall was 87.18%, 63.41%, and 76.92% for healthy controls, mild depression, and moderate-to-severe depression, respectively. At the participant level, reduced arm swing, slower pelvic movement, restricted joint range of motion, and greater arm-swing asymmetry were identified as leading potential digital biomarkers contributing to depression severity assessment, associated with higher 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for contactless digital depression severity stratification in adolescents. Further external and prospective validation is needed to establish their utility for longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical assessment.

items.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
items.summary: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

items.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
items.summary: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

items.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
items.summary: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.

items.title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking of Electrocardiogram Signals With Error-Correcting Codes
items.summary: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, making patient metadata vulnerable to loss. Digital watermarking embeds this metadata directly into the signal. However, conventional ECG watermarking methods fail under temporal desynchronization, and waveform similarity does not guarantee downstream diagnostic preservation. This article presents ECGWmark, a deep watermarking framework for single-lead ECG. A fully convolutional generator embeds the payload without signal quantization, a detector decodes the message frame by frame and verifies watermark presence, and a frozen arrhythmia classifier penalizes changes that would alter diagnostic predictions. To bridge the gap between bit accuracy and whole-message recovery, payloads are protected by extended Hamming codes, validation-selected interleaving, and soft-decision decoding. On the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, ECGWmark maintains over 90\% bit accuracy under time shifts of 10 to 50 samples, where transform baselines fall to chance level. With the coding layer, the protected 16-bit payload achieves 99.86\% exact recovery on clean segments and sustains over 90\% recovery under time shifts, 10\% sample deletion, and 10\% packet loss. Inter-patient evaluation confirms improved ventricular-beat sensitivity with preserved macro-F1. Requiring only 0.56 million parameters and about 15ms per segment on a desktop CPU, ECGWmark highlights the need to assess physiological watermarking through whole-message recovery and diagnostic consistency.

items.title: Integration of Ecological Momentary Assessment and Intervention With Wearable-Based Digital Phenotypes to Treat Anxiety in Young Adults: Mixed Methods Experimental Study
items.summary: Background: Young adults report high levels of anxiety, yet their access to timely treatment remains limited. Mobile-based digital therapeutics, particularly ecological momentary assessment and intervention (EMA/EMI), offer a promising approach to deliver context-responsive care. The integration of wearable-derived digital phenotypes with digital therapeutics may enhance the personalization of feedback in such interventions, but empirical evidence from real-world settings remains scarce. Objective: This study examined the real-world applicability and effectiveness of an EMA/EMI-based digital therapeutic, ANZEILAX-Green (HAII Corp), for use in anxiety reduction in young adults and investigated how personalized feedback generated by combining EMA/EMI data with wearable-based digital phenotypes ameliorates symptoms and promotes self-management and user engagement. Participants used a smartphone app in which EMA/EMI modules had been integrated with a smartwatch that continuously collected digital phenotyping data, including heart rate, sleep, and activity. Quantitative changes were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and repeated-measures ANOVA, and qualitative interviews were thematically analyzed to identify user experience mechanisms and design implications. items.title: Diagnostic performance of the ECG-SMART AI score for detecting angiographically significant coronary artery disease in patients undergoing elective coronary angiography
items.summary: by Dania A. Bani Hani, Jafar A. Alshraideh, Hamza Alduraidi, Akram Saleh, Nathan T. Riek, Karam Daoud, Rui Qi Ji, Samir Saba, Clifton W. Callaway, Salah Al-Zaiti The 12-lead ECG is central to the evaluation of patients with suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) but has limited diagnostic accuracy for identifying significant obstructive disease prior to elective coronary angiography. We previously developed an artificial intelligence–enhanced ECG (AI-ECG) model for detecting acute coronary occlusion. Whether this model generalizes to identifying angiographically significant CAD in symptomatic patients undergoing elective evaluation remains unknown. In this prospective cohort study, symptomatic outpatients undergoing elective coronary angiography at a tertiary center received standard 12-lead ECGs before the procedure. ECGs were analyzed offline using a previously validated AI-ECG model originally developed for acute coronary occlusion. Patients were categorized as low or intermediate-to-high risk using predefined thresholds. The primary outcome was angiographically significant CAD (≥70% stenosis in a major epicardial vessel or ≥50% stenosis of the left main coronary artery). Among 363 patients (age 58.9 ± 11 years; 55.1% male), 36.1% had angiographically significant CAD. The AI-ECG classified 56% as low risk and 44% as intermediate-to-high risk. items.title: A Group-Aware Comparative Study of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
items.summary: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearable or smartphone inertial sensors is commonly evaluated with both classical machine learning and deep learning methods. However, reported performance can be strongly affected by sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and data-splitting strategy. This study presents a controlled comparative evaluation of four classical machine learning models and four deep learning models on two public HAR datasets, UCI-HAR and KU-HAR. Three sensor modalities were considered: accelerometer (ACC), gyroscope (GYRO), and their combination (ACC+GYRO). Classical machine learning models used handcrafted statistical features, while deep learning models operated directly on raw sensor sequences. The primary evaluation employed five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold cross-validation, with subject- or participant-level grouping to prevent group overlap between training and test folds. Macro-F1 was used as the primary performance metric. The results show that deep learning did not consistently outperform classical machine learning. On UCI-HAR, the evaluated deep learning models achieved slightly higher macro-F1 values, whereas on KU-HAR, LightGBM achieved 0.857 compared with 0.828 for the highest-performing evaluated deep learning model. Regarding sensor modality, the combined ACC+GYRO configuration generally outperformed ACC or GYRO alone on both datasets. The evaluation protocol also had a substantial effect: for CNNBiLSTMAttn with ACC+GYRO, random splitting increased macro-F1 by 0.033 on UCI-HAR and 0.093 on KU-HAR compared with grouped evaluation. These findings highlight the importance of model family, sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and group-aware evaluation when assessing sensor-based HAR systems.

items.title: AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation
items.summary: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

items.title: BeatFlow-ECG: Rectified Flow for ECG Reconstruction from Indirect Wearable Signals
items.summary: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical to collect during daily life. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides rich information about cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology, while wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. We present BeatFlow-ECG, a conditional rectified-flow model for reconstructing single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements. BeatFlow-ECG models reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using a convolutional encoder-decoder with a transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning. Motion information is incorporated through IMU-derived conditioning features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and an easy-to-hard training curriculum. We evaluate the model under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD. BeatFlow-ECG achieves the best results among the evaluated deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines across all reported waveform and beat-timing metrics, with Pearson correlations of 0.983 and 0.986 and R-peak F1 scores of 0.946 and 0.955, respectively. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses on PPG-DaLiA show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

items.title: REFIT: Recognize, Fix, and Test Wearable Sensor Placement Shifts without Labels
items.summary: We present REFIT, an input calibration for frozen activity-recognition models whose inertial sensors are worn differently at deployment than in training. When users move a watch to the other wrist or put a strap sensor back on turned, the model sees the same motion on changed axes. REFIT undoes such shifts without labels or retraining. It describes them by families of axis transforms, such as reflections and rotations, and fits each family to the user's data so that simple statistics match those of the training data. The family that removes most of the mismatch names the shift. REFIT fixes the shift by applying the best member of that family before the frozen model and re-estimating its normalization statistics. It tests the fixed model with a label-free accuracy estimate and asks the user to re-wear the sensor when it is low. Experiments on real left/right sensor pairs and on real and simulated re-attachment show that REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset and restores most of the accuracy lost to re-attachment. It names injected shifts far more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After a correction over all signed permutations of the axes, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

items.title: Label-Efficient Deep Learning for ECG Delineation: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark against Widely Used Delineation Tools
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) delineation, the identification of waveform boundaries, is a foundational step that translates raw ECG signals into clinically interpretable measurements. Deep learning has advanced this task but remains dependent on costly expert annotations. Label-efficient strategies such as self-supervised pretraining and semi-supervised learning are expected to ease this burden, yet it remains unclear whether they yield reliable delineation and whether the deep models they produce outperform the delineation tools used in practice. We address this in two stages. First, comparing self-supervised objectives with supervised or semi-supervised fine-tuning across one internal and four external datasets, we find that pretraining helps but the objective matters, and that the value of semi-supervised fine-tuning depends on the pretraining objective. Second, we benchmark the selected deep learning model against widely used open-source (NeuroKit2, Prominence, ECGdeli) and commercial (CalECG) tools using three complementary metrics. The model ranks best on every metric and dataset, outperforming the strongest tool by a clear margin on the rhythm-diverse set (mIoU 71.3 vs. 54.8%; averaged point-wise sensitivity 92.6 vs. 76.4%), and degrades the least from sinus to arrhythmia. A rhythm-stratified and point-wise analysis further characterizes the distinctive behavior of each tool, yielding practical guidance for tool selection. These results provide systematic, multi-dataset evidence that self-supervised pretraining is effective for ECG delineation and enables a label-efficiently trained deep learning model to outperform widely used delineation tools by leveraging abundant unlabeled data. This supports adopting such models in diverse, real-world clinical settings.

items.title: Characterizing the Performance Gap in Human Activity Recognition for Older Adults
items.summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn accelerometers is increasingly used for health and behavioral tracking. Yet, most wearable HAR models are developed and evaluated on datasets dominated by younger adults, leaving it unclear whether benchmark progress generalizes across age groups. In this work, we leverage MyMove, our carefully annotated, free-living older-adult HAR dataset (mean age 71), to evaluate deep-learning architectures and training regimes under both leave-one-subject-out and cross-dataset transfer. We find that improvements on younger-adult benchmarks fail to transfer equally to data collected from older adults, resulting in a persistent and often widening performance gap. However, richer representations, particularly frozen self-supervised features pretrained on the age-diverse UK Biobank dataset, substantially improve performance on data from older adults and consistently narrow the performance gap, at modest cost to younger-adult performance, though disparities remain. These findings suggest that benchmark gains and architectural scaling alone provide an incomplete picture of progress in wearable HAR, and broader advances may require representations that better capture population diversity, alongside personalized adaptation to individual movement patterns and routines.

items.title: Open-Source Multi-Wire SPI Readout for Wearable Ultrasound Probes
items.summary: Wearable ultrasound probes must transfer increasingly large acquisition payloads while maintaining compact, low-power electronics. In TinyProbe, the current bottleneck in data transfer occurs between the acquisition FPGA and the wireless system controller. This work presents an open-source, multi-wire SPI readout interface that uses serial command and address phases followed by a build-time-selectable dual- or quad-lane payload phase that is intended to address this bottleneck by increasing the potential bandwidth over the wifi limit while retaining compatibility with the Microcontroller-centric wearable US architecture. The interface emulates a serial flash memory, enabling compatibility with a broad range of microcontroller families and their existing peripheral interfaces. On the FPGA, the data path connects the existing acquisition FIFOs to the SPI interface through clock-domain crossing, sample reshaping, and packing into 32-bit words. Dual-SPI readout is integrated into the existing IGLOO2/SiWG917 TinyProbe architecture and verified at an SCLK frequency of 5 MHz. A separate Kria K26 testbed is used to characterize the FPGA SPI interface independently of the acquisition and wireless subsystems, demonstrating error-free transfers at SCLK frequencies up to 66 MHz. These measurements identify the SiWG917 multi-lane SPI implementation as the next bandwidth-limiting component and motivate a future upgrade of the system controller. The HDL and MCU implementations are released under a permissive open-source license.

items.title: One Sensor, Whole Body - 3D Body Pose from a Single Consumer Earbud IMU
items.summary: Consumer earbuds already stream inertial motion data from the head, one of the most widely worn sensor locations on the body. We ask how much of the 3D body pose a single such head IMU can recover, and whether adding more consumer sensors actually helps. We build a multimodal capture pipeline that records four-view RGB-D video together with an AirPods head IMU and two Striv insole IMUs, synchronize the streams post-hoc, and generate pseudo-ground-truth with SAM 3D Body, yielding a 35-take single-subject benchmark spanning gait, turning, vertical, everyday, and clinically inspired motions. Adapting two recurrent model families (IMUPoser and MobilePoser), we show that one head IMU recovers lower-body pose at 79.0 mm rigid-MPJPE and per-foot ground contact at 0.809 macro-F1, and that a causal variant retains most of this accuracy at streaming latency. In paired per-take significance tests across both families, adding the consumer foot IMUs never significantly improves pose and significantly degrades it in two of four model-split combinations; a mounting-bias probe and feet-only ablation identify insole orientation quality, not foot placement, as the mechanism. Extending the output to a 20-joint full-body skeleton maps the boundary: gross distal-arm motion is partially recoverable from the head alone, proximal upper-body pose is not, and staged fine-tuning recovers the leg accuracy that naive joint training sacrifices to multi-task dilution. For learned pose from consumer wearables, sensor reliability, not sensor count, is the binding constraint here. For the devices tested, the earbud is its sweet spot. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhilinGuo/one-sensor-whole-body.

items.title: ECG-Scroll: A Long-Horizon, Streaming Benchmark and Agent Environment for Interpretation of Ambulatory Electrocardiograms
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now interpret a standard ten-second, twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with clinically grounded, reward-verified reasoning. Real cardiac monitoring is different. Ambulatory (Holter) and telemetry recordings span hours to days and are read as they stream in, and their clinically decisive findings are paroxysmal, brief episodes buried in an otherwise unremarkable trace. Such a recording cannot be held in one context at diagnostic resolution, and its future has not yet happened, so a reader must work online, deciding what to measure now, committing evidence to memory as it passes, and reporting events as they occur. We recast long-duration ECG interpretation as a long-horizon, online (streaming, causal) sequential decision process and introduce ECG-Scroll. As a benchmark, long ambulatory recordings are streamed to an agent chunk by chunk, and it must localize, quantify, and promptly flag paroxysmal events without access to future signal; because the underlying signal is retained, every answer is checkable against objective ground truth, giving rule-based rather than judge-based rewards, and the streaming formulation adds a metric batch evaluation cannot express, the detection latency between an event's onset and the moment the agent records it. As an agent environment, it is a fixed, gym-style interaction layer that exercises three competencies single-glance ECG models never touch: Memory, Tool use through signal-grounded measurement rather than reading pixels, and Planning of what to measure now and when to commit. We release 390 whole-recording instances spanning 2,536 hours of two-lead ambulatory ECG and evaluate a signal-threshold rule agent alongside off-the-shelf LLM agents online, characterizing how they use memory, tools, and planning and where the benchmark's head-room lies.

academic.title: Glucoregulatory and Inflammatory Trajectories in Pregnancy with Obesity: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Exercise Trial
academic.summary: Objective: To evaluate moderate-intensity exercise effects on glucoregulatory and inflammatory markers in pregnant women with obesity. Methods: Secondary analysis of the Expecting Study (NCT02125149) included 263 sedentary pregnant women with pre-pregnancy BMI [>=]30kg/m2 randomized to exercise (EX, n=157) or standard-of-care (SoC, n=106). Fasting biomarkers were assessed at 12.14{+/-}0.50, 24.19{+/-}0.68, and 36.03{+/-}0.58 weeks ' gestation. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated intervention and gestational effects at 24-36 weeks. Exploratory repeated-measures continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) included 18 participants (SoC=6, EX=12), evaluating 24-h/temporal glycemia and exploring inflammatory marker associations. Results: Insulin, C-peptide, HOMA2-IR, HOMA2-%B, IL-6, and TNF- increased with gestation, while HOMA2-%S and CRP decreased (all p 95% valid wear time; glycemia remained normoglycemic. By 36-weeks, SoC-metrics declined in 24-h and nocturnal glucose and time-in-range (TIR), with increased time-below-range (all p<0.022). TIR was inversely associated with IL-6 at 24-weeks (-0.23 [95%CI: -0.43,-0.02] p=0.035), and mean amplitude of glycemic excursion positively with TNF- at 36-weeks (0.02 [95%CI: 0.00,0.04] p=0.033). Conclusion: Exercise did not modify mid-to late-gestation fasting glucoregulatory or inflammatory profiles. High CGM-adherence and preliminary indications of distinct longitudinal glycemic patterns support further CGM evaluation in antepartum behavioral interventions.

academic.title: Digital Twin Workflow for Continuous Glucose Forecasting: Real-Time Data Assimilation Using Reinforcement Learning
academic.summary: Digital twins for physiological forecasting require robust mechanisms for continuously assimilating streaming data and adapting to patient-specific dynamics. Threshold-triggered model updates can restore predictive performance after substantial drift, but their reactive nature limits continuous adaptation. We propose a proactive digital twin framework that couples a pretrained PatchTST foundation model with an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning (RL) agent for residual correction. Using a 30-minute look-back window and recent residual history, the agent generates bounded corrections ({+/-} 0.05) to the first-step baseline forecast, with corrected predictions recursively propagated over a 15-step horizon. We evaluate both an RL-only workflow and a hybrid workflow combining RL correction with threshold-triggered fine-tuning using minute-by-minute continuous glucose monitoring data from 10 critically ill patients with sepsis. Across all patients, the pretrained RL agent improves forecasting accuracy without patient-specific retraining. Both workflows reduce trajectory-averaged mean absolute percentage error, ensemble relative error, and maximum errors compared with the uncorrected baseline and previously developed reactive digital twin models. These findings support residual reinforcement learning as a lightweight mechanism for continuous, real-time data assimilation that preserves the foundation model's global predictive prior while enabling patient-specific forecast adaptation, with potential applications in critical care decision support.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6742: A Feasibility Study for Integrating Schumann Resonance Monitoring, Geomagnetic Activity Indices, and Large-Scale Ambulatory ECG Databases: Toward Synchronized Environmental-Physiological Research
academic.summary: Schumann resonance (SR) is a global electromagnetic phenomenon generated within the Earth-ionosphere cavity, with a fundamental frequency near 7.83 Hz. Whether SR dynamics are associated with human autonomic nervous system activity as indexed by heart rate variability (HRV) remains an open empirical question. Addressing this question rigorously requires (a) large-scale, time-synchronized physiological datasets, (b) continuous SR monitoring with precise timestamps, and (c) control for geomagnetic activity (Kp index) as a major confounding variable. Currently available open datasets do not yet satisfy condition (a). Rather than forcing premature physiological conclusions, this paper presents a feasibility and methodology study that characterizes each data source, demonstrates the analysis pipeline on representative data, and identifies the design requirements for a future definitive study. Frequency-domain HRV indices were characterized using approximately 730,000 24-h Holter ECG recordings from the Allostatic State Mapping by Ambulatory ECG Repository (ALLSTAR). Broadband voltage SD (segment-wise standard deviation of AC-coupled voltage, used solely as a descriptive amplitude proxy) was characterized using the publicly available Mendeley Schumann Resonance Dataset (35 min segments, 525,000 samples each). A partial correlation framework that controls for the NOAA Kp geomagnetic index is proposed and evaluated through simulation on representative parameter sets. Because the HRV and SR datasets were not collected at the same time or location, no direct physiological inference is drawn from their comparison. The reported association statistics are illustrative demonstrations of the pipeline applied to representative data, not empirical evidence of SR-HRV coupling. These findings define the data requirements and analytical methodology for future synchronized SR-HRV-Kp studies.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6710: An ESP32-S3 Multimodal Wearable Sensor Platform with Embedded XGBoost for Focal-to-Bilateral Tonic-Clonic Seizure Detection and IoT Alerting
academic.summary: Wearable seizure-detection systems can provide objective event monitoring and rapid caregiver alerting without continuous bedside observation. This study presents a resource-constrained multimodal wearable sensor platform for focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (FBTCS) detection using edge artificial intelligence and Internet of Things (IoT) communication. The prototype integrates an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, an analog electromyography (EMG) channel, an MPU6050 inertial sensor, MAX30102 photoplethysmography, GPS, a TFT display, local vibration/buzzer outputs, and Blynk cloud telemetry. The seizure-decision path uses synchronized EMG and acceleration acquired at 100 Hz in non-overlapping 10 s windows. EMG and acceleration are resampled for compatibility with the reference feature pipeline, 13 statistical features are extracted from each modality (26 total), and an 85-tree XGBoost model is executed locally. A probability threshold of 0.85 is combined with temporal smoothing, consecutive-window confirmation, and a 60 s refractory interval. Software verification showed maximum absolute probability differences of approximately 1.19 x 10-7 for random feature-vector tests and 1.49 x 10-8 for end-to-end recorded windows relative to the Python reference. Within the reported validation record covering 2643.69 h and 18 record-labeled FBTCS events, 12 events were detected (12/18; 67% sensitivity). Precision was approximately 26%, F1-score approximately 38%, the reported false-alarm rate was 0.31 per 24 h, and median detection latency was 61.5 s. Approximately 34 false alarms are estimated from the reported false-alarm rate and evaluation duration; this is an estimated count rather than a percentage or directly observed count. Hardware, local alarm, display, GPS, and cloud communication functions passed functional integration tests. The small event count, uncertain label provenance, low precision, and long latency mean that these data support an engineering proof-of-concept

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6670: The Case for Low-Friction High-Adherence Passive Sleep-Tracking Devices in Longitudinal Monitoring of Neurodegenerative Disease
academic.summary: Digital health technologies are playing an increasingly important role in patient monitoring, able to capture longitudinal data to supplement scheduled episodic evaluations conducted by clinicians. Rapid advances in sensors and data processing algorithms have resulted in some highly sophisticated systems capable of monitoring and tracking numerous symptoms with high levels of sensitivity and specificity. These approaches, however, often require active engagement with the patient, potentially increasing burden in a clinical trial and often resulting in diminishing adherence over time. In the case of slow-progressing neurodegenerative diseases, this may become an obstacle, as often very subtle changes in symptoms are typically monitored over a multi-year period. Accordingly, there is evident interest in passive monitoring solutions which have minimal burden on patients. Smart ring technologies are one such solution, with appealing form factors, low engagement requirements and increasing intervals before device recharging is required. While newer devices are capable of tracking sleep function with increasing levels of accuracy, they are unable to offer the precision afforded by gold standard sleep analysis such as electroencephalography (EEG), polysomnography (PSG) and sleep laboratory protocols. Prompted by a recent study which highlighted the reduced accuracy of consumer-based sleep devices compared with conventional approaches, we posit that the benefits of such devices may offset the constraints of measurement accuracy. Furthermore, any accuracy-adherence trade-offs would be compensated by long-term statistical benefits derived from detecting within-person changes and reducing measurement noise through enhanced sampling frequencies. academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6683: A Human-in-the-Loop Reference-Label Curation Framework for Task Classification During Free-Living, Using 3D Animation of IMU Data
academic.summary: Reference-labelled data for training activity-recognition models from wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) are typically collected in laboratories, which poorly represent real-world movement, and often use video, which raises privacy concerns and does not scale to long recordings. This study evaluated a novel human-in-the-loop annotation framework in which IMU-derived skeletal animations are reviewed by human raters to generate activity labels. Eight participants performed 72 functional tasks in a simulated living environment while wearing IMUs, with synchronized video serving as a reference standard. Data from five participants were analyzed. Two reviewers labelled both IMU animations and video recordings, and intra- and inter-reviewer agreement were compared across a detailed label set and a simplified four-class taxonomy. Using the video annotations as the reference standard, the intra-reviewer macro-averaged F1 for the detailed label set was 61.9 +/- 13.5% (Cohen's = 0.67 +/- 0.12), and 78.0 +/- 11.5% ( = 0.74 +/- 0.13) for the simplified taxonomy. In a sensitivity analysis excluding samples labelled as transitions, macro-F1 was 69.4 +/- 10.9% and 92.8 +/- 5.3%, respectively. Inter-reviewer agreement for the detailed label set was lower when labelling animations ( = 0.51 +/- 0.06) than video ( = 0.72 +/- 0.02). A main source of disagreement between reviewers was in the labelling of transitions of state, reflecting in part the ambiguous nature of defining their endpoints. These findings support skeletal-animation review as a potential privacy-preserving alternative to video annotation for generating reference labels in simulated living; validation in free-living recordings, and of the reconstructed kinematics, is still required.

academic.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
academic.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6665: A Multimodal IMU-RTLS Manufacturing Motion Dataset for Worker Activity Recognition
academic.summary: Worker Activity Recognition can improve operational visibility in human-centric manufacturing systems. However, existing approaches remain limited by scarce industrial datasets, isolated task recordings, and sensor-intensive configurations. This study presents two multimodal datasets and a cyber-physical architecture for complementary levels of worker motion. The Gross Worker Activity Recognition dataset targets operator proximity to workstation and the identification of logistic activities in reconfigurable manufacturing systems. It contains 814,065 positioning samples from eight production setups, each repeated twice, involving more than 40 workers. This dataset is benchmarked with different learning structure algorithms, and the Long Short-Term Memory is selected as a baseline model, achieving an F1-score of 86%. The Fine Worker Activity Recognition dataset targets the segmentation of five pump-assembly operations using two inertial measurement units and a radio-frequency-identification smart glove. It comprises approximately 7 h of recordings and more than one million samples from 50 complete assemblies performed by three workers. Transformer, ResNet, and SqueezeNet models are benchmarked, with SqueezeNet selected as the baseline after achieving the highest F1-score of 85.2%. Moreover, the results identify transition-rich activities as the principal recognition bottleneck and show how complementary motion levels support different manufacturing indicators.

academic.title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
academic.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

academic.title: ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health
academic.summary: Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.
